title: Sanjana Jon vs Pawan Kumar Singh on 13 October, 2025
full_text: Sanjana Jon vs Pawan Kumar Singh on 13 October, 2025 IN THE COURT OF Ms. AASTHA SHARMA, LD. JMFC (N.I. Act)-03, SOUTH-EAST DISTRICT, SAKET COURTS COMPLEX: DELHI Sanjana Jon Vs. Pawan Kumar CC No. 634842/2016 U/S 138 Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 1. CNR number DLSE02-009923-2016 2. Name of the complainant Ms. Sanjana Jon R/o B-321, Anand Lok Part-1, Gurgaon, Haryana 3. Name of the accused person(s), parentage & Mr. Pawan Kumar Singh residential address R/o WZ-510A, Palam Village, Opposite Chottu Ram Public School, South-West Delhi, New Delhi-110077 Also at: 14, Bishunapura, Town/ Village - Sherapur, Anchal - Maraurha, Distt - Saran, Bihar CC No. 634842/2016 Sanjana Jon vs. Pawan Kumar Page 1 of 14 Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA AASTHA Date: SHARMA 2025.10.13 17:24:07 +0530 4. Offence complained of or proved U/s 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 5. Plea of the accused Pleaded not guilty and claimed trial 6. Final Judgment/order 13.10.2025 7. Date of judgment/order 13.10.2025 Date of Institution: 12.07.2016 Date of Reserving Judgment/Order: 09.09.2025 Date of Pronouncement of Judgment/Order: 13.10.2025 ARGUING COUNSELS: Ld. Counsel for the complainant: Sh. Ravi Bhushan Upadhyay Ld. LAC for the Accused: Sh. Vipin Chaudhary. JUDGMENT 1. Vide this judgment, this Court shall dispose of the present complaint filed by the complainant Ms. Sanjana Jon through SPA Holder Sh. Abhishek Saha (hereinafter referred CC No. 634842/2016 Sanjana Jon vs. Pawan Kumar Page 2 of 14 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.10.13 17:24:20 +0530 to as "the Complainant") against Sh. Pawan Kumar Singh (hereinafter referred to as "the Accused"), under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 read with Section 142 of Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (hereinafter referred to as " NI Act "). Brief facts of the case: 2. It is the case of the complainant, A. That, the complainant is Fashion Designer, Entrepreneur and a social worker and the accused used to work at her office/residence. That, the accused approached the complainant and requested her for a friendly loan of Rs. 5,00,000/- for purchasing the house i.e. WZ-510A, Palam Village, Opposite Chottu Ram Public, School South West Delhi, New Delhi-110077. That, at the time of advancing aforesaid amount of Rs. 5,00,000/- to the accused, sister of the accused namely Beena Devi had given undertaken to pay the loan amount in case of default by the accused and further it was mentioned in the said undertaking that in case the accused leaves his job, the entire amount will be paid immediately before termination of employment. Further, the accused undertook to pay the aforesaid loan amount to the complainant within a period of one year and the same was mentioned in an agreement placed on record as well. B. That, in furtherance of the commitment of the accused towards the complainant, the accused had issued a cheque bearing no. 510870 dated 04.09.2015 for an amount of Rs. 5,00,000/- drawn at State Bank of India, 151-Seth Square Building, Palam Road, Sector-7, Dwarka, New Delhi-110075, in favour of the complainant and he had assured the complainant that the cheque would be honored at the time of its presentation. CC No. 634842/2016 Sanjana Jon vs. Pawan Kumar Page 3 of 14 Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA AASTHA Date: SHARMA 2025.10.13 17:24:30 +0530 C. That, on assurance of the accused person, the complainant had presented the aforesaid cheque for encashment with his banker namely Citibank, South Extension, New Delhi, however the cheque was returned dishonoured with the remarks "Funds Insufficient" vide returning memo dated 16.09.2015. D. In these circumstances, the complainant got issued a statutory legal demand notice to the accused through his counsel, dated 15.10.2015, thereby requiring the accused to pay the amount of the aforesaid cheque within a period of 15 days from the receipt of the said notice. The said notice under Sec. 138 of NI Act was sent to the accused through Registered AD/Speed Post/Courier at his correct address on 17.10.2015. That despite service of the above stated notice of demand, the Accused has deliberately and willfully failed to comply with the said notice of demand and has failed to pay the amount of the aforesaid cheque within the stipulated period of 15 days from the date of receipt of the said notice. Consequently, this case was filed by the complainant against the accused, which was within the limitation period as laid down u/s 138 , NI Act. 3. In the pre-summoning evidence, the Authorised representative of the complainant Sh.Vivek Karnatak examined himself on affidavit being Ex. CW1/9 and placed on record Copy of Special Power of Attorney in his favour Ex. CW-1/1; Original undertaking given by sister of accused namely Ms. Beena Devi Ex. CW-1/2; Cheque in question is exhibited Ex. CW1/3; Cheque return memo Ex. CW1/4; Legal demand notice Ex. CW1/5; Speed Post receipts Ex. CW1/6 & Ex. CW-1/7 and Tracking/ delivery report Ex. CW-1/8. 4. Upon prima facie consideration of the pre-summoning evidence, the accused person was summoned. CC No. 634842/2016 Sanjana Jon vs. Pawan Kumar Page 4 of 14 Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA AASTHA Date: SHARMA 2025.10.13 17:24:40 +0530 5. Upon the appearance of the accused, notice under Section 251 CrPC was served upon him on 25.01.2023 to which he pleaded not guilty. At this stage, the accused admitted that he had issued the cheque in question and also admitted his signatures therein. He has denied receiving the legal demand notice. He stated that he had returned the cheque amount to the complainant in installments through cash which was received by the complainant after executing receipt by complainant from time to time. He has further stated that he had also given possession of his motorcycle no. DL-03-SBK-5951 to the complainant towards security along with the blank cheque in question at the time of availing loan which is still in possession of the complainant till date. 6. CW-1 was examined-in-chief, cross-examined and discharged. Thereby, CE was closed on 27.07.2023. Accordingly, the matter proceeded to the stage of recording the statement of the accused. 7. Statement of accused under Section 313 CrPC read with Section 281 CrPC was recorded on 16.08.2023 wherein the accused opted to lead defence evidence, and examined himself as DW-1. An application u/s 315 CrPC was moved on behalf of the accused for examination of the accused as DW-1 which was allowed by this Hon'ble court in the interest of justice vide order dated 04.04.2024. DW-1 was examined, cross-examined and discharged. Further, DW-2 was examined, cross-examined and discharged. DE was closed vide order of this court by recording a separate statement of the accused on 30.07.2025. 8. Thereafter, the matter was listed for final arguments. After hearing the final arguments from both sides and on the basis of the written submissions on record by both the parties, the matter was reserved for pronouncement of judgment. CC No. 634842/2016 Sanjana Jon vs. Pawan Kumar Page 5 of 14 Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA AASTHA Date: SHARMA 2025.10.13 17:24:49 +0530 9. It is well settled position of law that to constitute an offence under Section 138 , NI Act, the following ingredients are required to be fulfilled: I. drawing of the cheque by a person on an account maintained by him with a banker, II. The cheque was issued for payment to another person for discharge in whole/part any debt or liability; III. Cheque has been presented to the bank within a period of six months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity whichever is earlier. RBI in its notification DBOD.AML BC.No.47/14.01.001/2011-12 has reduced the aforesaid period from 6 months to 3 months. IV. Returning of the cheque unpaid by the drawee bank for want of sufficient funds to the credit of the drawer or any arrangement with the banker to pay the sum covered by the cheque; V. Giving notice in writing to the drawer of the cheque within 30 days of the receipt of information by the payee from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid demanding payment of the cheque amount; VI. Failure of the drawer to make payment to the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque, of the amount covered by the cheque within 15 days of the receipt of the notice. The offence under Section 138 , NI Act is made out against the drawer of the cheque, only when all the aforementioned ingredients are fulfilled. CC No. 634842/2016 Sanjana Jon vs. Pawan Kumar Page 6 of 14 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.10.13 17:25:01 +0530 10. Analysing all the concerned provisions of law and various pronouncements in this regard, the Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Basalingappa v. Mudibasappa [AIR 2019 SC 1983] held that: I. Once the execution of cheque is admitted, Section 139 of the Act mandates that a presumption be drawn that the cheque in question was for the discharge of any debt or other liability. II. The presumption under Section 139 is a rebuttable presumption and the onus is on the accused to raise the probable defence. The standard of proof for rebutting the presumption is that of preponderance of probabilities. III. To rebut the presumption, it is open for the accused to rely on evidence led by him or accused can also rely on the materials submitted by the complainant in order to raise a probable defence. Inference of preponderance of probabilities can be drawn not only from the materials brought on record by reference to the circumstances upon which they rely. IV. That it is not necessary for the accused to come in the witness box in support of his defence. Section 139 imposes an evidentiary burden and not a persuasive burden. It is therefore implied that the law regarding the presumption for the offence under Section 138 , NI Act, the presumptions under Section 118(a) and Section 139 have to be compulsorily raised as soon as the execution of cheque by the accused is admitted or proved by the complainant and thereafter the burden is shifted upon the accused to prove otherwise. CC No. 634842/2016 Sanjana Jon vs. Pawan Kumar Page 7 of 14 Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA AASTHA Date: SHARMA 2025.10.13 17:25:13 +0530 Appreciation of evidence and marshalling of facts: 11. Issuance of cheque: The complainant has filed on record the original cheque, i.e., bearing no. 510870 dated 04.09.2015 for Rs. 5,00,000/- drawn on State Bank of India, Sector 7, Dwarka (Ex. CW1/3). In notice under Section 251 CrPC, the accused has admitted that the cheque in dispute belongs to him. It is also not disputed that the cheque in question is not drawn on the account maintained by the accused person and it is impliedly admitted therefore that the accused is the drawer of the cheque. Therefore, ingredient number I stands fulfilled in the present case. 12. Presentment and dishonor of cheque: As per the RBI guidelines, it is essential for the cheque in question be to presented within a period of three months from the date on which they are drawn and the same be returned as unpaid by the drawee bank for want of sufficient funds to the credit of the drawer or any arrangement with the banker to pay the sum covered by the cheque. In the case at hand, the cheques in question were returned vide return memo dated 16.09.2015 (Ex. CW1/4) due to the reason "Funds Insufficient." By implication thereof, the cheque was presented within three months and the same was returned. Therefore, Ingredient number III & IV stand fulfilled in the present case. 13. Legal demand notice and payment by the accused thereof: The legal notice dated 15.10.2015 (Ex. CW1/5) was dispatched on 15.10.2015 vide Speed Post (Ex. CW1/6), i.e., within 30 days of return of the bank memo indicating cheques in question being unpaid. The fact that the legal demand notice has made a clear and unambiguous demand for payment of the cheque in question is not disputed. The accused has denied the receiving of legal demand notice in notice u/s 251 CrPC. However, as per the presumption raised under CC No. 634842/2016 Sanjana Jon vs. Pawan Kumar Page 8 of 14 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.10.13 17:25:23 +0530 Section 114 of Indian Evidence Act, 1872 and Section 27 of General Clauses Act, if the legal demand notice is sent at the correct address, then the same shall be deemed to have been duly served, as per the precedent laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in C.C. Alavi Haji v. Palapetty Muhammed , (2007) 3 SCC (Cri). The ingredient number V is fulfilled by virtue of giving of legal demand notice within 30 days from the bank return memo. The receipt of legal demand notice by the accused is deemed to be admitted as per the discussion above. 14. Moving on, it is not disputed that the accused has not made the payment of the cheque amount within 15 days of the receipt of legal demand notice. Therefore, ingredient number VI also stands fulfilled in the present case. Presumption under Section 118A read with Section 139 , NI Act 15. The NI Act raises two presumptions in favour of the holder of the cheque, i.e., complainant; firstly, with regard to the issuance of cheque for consideration, as contained in Section 118(a) and secondly, with regard to the fact that the holder of cheque received the same for discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability, as contained in Section 139 of the Act. These presumptions shall end only when the contrary is proved by the accused, that is, the cheque was not issued for consideration and in discharge of any debt or liability etc. The Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in its judgment titled Rangappa Vs. Sri Mohan , (2010) 11 SCC 441 held that a reverse onus clause usually imposes an evidentiary burden and not a persuasive burden and when an accused has to rebut the presumption under Section 139 , the standard of proof for doing so is that of "preponderance of probabilities". Therefore, if the accused is able to raise a probable defence which creates doubts about the CC No. 634842/2016 Sanjana Jon vs. Pawan Kumar Page 9 of 14 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.10.13 17:25:33 +0530 existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability, the prosecution can fail. It was further held that the accused can rely on the materials submitted by the complainant in order to raise such a defence and it is conceivable that in some cases the accused may not need to adduce evidence of his/her own. Once a probable defence is raised, then the onus is shifted to the complainant to establish that a legally enforceable liability existed in his favour and the burden of proof on the complainant in this case is that of "beyond reasonable doubt." 16. The accused can rebut the presumption as raised under Section 138 , NI Act by: (a) putting forth his defence at the time of framing of notice u/s 251 CrPC; (b) cross-examining the complainant; (c) when statement of accused is recorded u/s 313 CrPC; (d) or by leading defence evidence, thereby demolishing the case of the complainant. Rebuttal of Presumption by Accused as to existence of legally enforceable debt 17. In light of the above discussion, since the accused has admitted to issuance of cheques, admitted the signatures on the cheques and legal notice has also been deemed to be served, what is left to be seen is whether the accused has been able to rebut the presumption against him, i.e., whether the accused is able to raise a probable defence which creates doubts about the existence of a legally enforceable debt? 18. In the present case, in order to discharge his initial burden to prove the abovementioned ingredients, the complainant relied upon the affidavit of the complainant being Ex. CW1/9 and placed on record documents mentioned hereinbefore. The primary defence of the accused is that he has returned the cheque amount to the complainant in installments CC No. 634842/2016 Sanjana Jon vs. Pawan Kumar Page 10 of 14 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.10.13 17:25:43 +0530 through cash which was received by the complainant and receipts were also issued by the complainant qua the same. The accused has been consistent in his defence at the stage of notice u/s 251 CrPC, statement of accused u/s 313 CrPC and at the stage of DE. 19. The case of the complainant is that the accused was in her employment and had borrowed a sum of Rs. 5,00,000/- from the complainant for which the guarantee was undertaken by the sister of the accused. Further, the complainant in her complaint has stated that she had also advanced a loan of Rs. 5,90,000/- to the wife of the accused. It is to be noted that the complainant has taken contradictory stances in her testimony as CW-1, wherein she has stated as follows: "...It is wrong to suggest that prior to loan in question, no loan was ever given to the accused. I have not given any loan to sister of the accused. (Vol. I had given loan to Ms. Beena, sister of the accused). I am having proof of lending loan to Ms. Beena, sister of the accused. I have not filed the document showing proof of loan lending to sister of accused on record, however, I can bring the same." "....Ques: I put it you on how many occasions Ms. Beena Devi have given you money in any form? Ans. Ms. Beena Devi returned the loan which was taken by her from me. I do not remember in how much installments, she had returned the entire loan amount..." "I have not disclose about the loan given to Ms. Beena Devi in this case or in legal notice given to the accused. I gave loan to Ms. Beena Devi in and about the same time when I had given loan to accused Pawan Kumar Singh when they needed money for purchase of house. I am USA resident, so did not pay income tax in India at that time. I do not remember who CC No. 634842/2016 Sanjana Jon vs. Pawan Kumar Page 11 of 14 Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA AASTHA Date: SHARMA 2025.10.13 17:25:54 +0530 was present there when I advanced loan to accused Pawan Kumar Singh and to Ms. Beena Devi..." The complainant in her complaint and evidence by way of affidavit has stated that she had advanced the loan to the accused and his wife, while at the stage of her testimony as CW-1, she stated that she had advanced the loan to the accused and her sister Beena Devi. She has herself admitted that she did not disclose about the loan to Beena Devi in her complaint or the legal demand notice. Furthermore, the complainant has stated that she can bring proof regarding loan transactions between the complainant and the sister of the accused, however she has not placed anything on record to prove the same. 20. Furthermore, it is admitted by the complainant as well that Ms. Beena Devi, i.e., sister of the accused acted as a guarantor to the loan taken by accused Pawan Kumar Singh. The complainant in her testimony has stated as follows: "It is correct that as per document Ex. CW1/2, Ms. Beena Devi (sister of accused) was guarantor of loan which was given to accused Pawan Kumar Singh.." "..It is wrong to suggest that the said money was returned on behalf of the accused Pawan Kumar Singh as she undertook to pay the liabilities of accused Pawan Kumar Singh as per agreement Ex. CW1/2. It is wrong to suggest that the loan taken by accused Pawan Kumar Singh was returned by her sister Ms. Beena Devi. It is wrong to suggest that I did not advance separate loan to Ms. Beena Devi..." "..At this stage, witness is shown four original receipts of refund of loan, upon which the witness admits out of four receipts only one receipt Ex. CW-1/D-1 is admitted. The witness states that other reciept Ex. CW-1/D-2 dated 10.07.2016 is not written in her handwriting CC No. 634842/2016 Sanjana Jon vs. Pawan Kumar Page 12 of 14 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.10.13 17:26:05 +0530 nor signed by her. Qua receipts dated 11.08.2016 and 14.09.2016, Ex. CW-1/D-3 and Ex. CW-1/D-4 respectively, the witness states that she cannot recollect whether the said receipts were written or signed by her.." On one hand, the complainant is admitting to Beena Devi standing as a guarantor to the accused and on the other hand, she is denying that the payment made by Beena Devi was towards the loan advanced to the accused. The complainant is further denying the cash receipts Ex. CW-1/D-2 to Ex. CW-1/D-4. However, as soon as the accused confronted the complainant with the receipts Ex. CW-1/D-1 to Ex. CW-1/D-4 issued by the complainant in favour of the sister of the accused who acted as a guarantor for the accused, presumption u/s 139 , NI Act stood rebutted because the accused person raised a probable defence. The onus then shifted upon the complainant to bring oral or documentary evidence to prove beyond reasonable doubt that the sister of accused had also borrowed a loan from the complainant and the receipts were issued for the repayment qua the same and not for the loan taken by the accused from the complainant. However, the complainant has failed to bring anything to corroborate his case. 21. In view of the aforesaid findings and analysis, this court has arrived at an irresistible conclusion that the accused has been able to cast a shadow of reasonable doubt upon the case of the complainant by rebutting the mandatory presumption resting in its favour and by several inconsistencies in the version of the complainant. Once the accused had created a probable defence as to the legally enforceable liability, the onus shifted on the complainant to prove the existence of legally enforceable liability of the accused, as on the date of the drawal or presentation of the impugned cheques, which has not been fulfilled by the complainant in the present case. Since this basic ingredient which is pivotal to attract CC No. 634842/2016 Sanjana Jon vs. Pawan Kumar Page 13 of 14 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.10.13 17:26:17 +0530 liability under Section 138 NI Act has not been proved by the complainant, accordingly, no offence of dishonour of the impugned cheque under the said Section is made out. 22. In light of the discussion above, ingredient no. II has not been fulfilled in the present case. Conclusion: 23. In view of the aforesaid discussion, the accused Pawan Kumar has been successful in establishing a probable defence on a standard of preponderance of probabilities to rebut the presumption under Section 118 and 139 of the NI Act by punching holes in the case of the complainant and making the case of the complainant doubtful. The accused has been successful in establishing a probable defence and as a consequence, questioning the existence of legally enforceable liability in favour of the complainant and that the cheque was not issued by the accused in discharge of existing legally enforceable debt or liability owed to the complainant. In the result of the analysis of the present case, the accused Pawan Kumar is hereby acquitted of the offence punishable under Section 138 , Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881.
